note: Discovery leads for political-science topic workers (phase 4). LITERACY level: general. NO policy positions; NO partisan advocacy; U.S. government structure taught factually per primary sources; comparative politics descriptive; contested topics (ideology, civil liberties, public opinion) presented with attributed sources and both-sides factual framing. All examples ORIGINAL (fictional people/scenarios). Tier A anchors: OpenStax American Government 3e (openstax.org blocks direct fetch → Wayback captures of canonical URLs; LibreTexts mirror OK), USA.gov / whitehouse.gov / congress.gov / supremecourt.gov (live or Wayback), U.S. Constitution & Bill of Rights (constitution.congress.gov — live, authoritative), Congressional Research Service reports, Pew Research Center (live), Gallup (live), Library of Congress. Tier B: Britannica, SEP, C-SPAN classroom. Registry check FIRST: the sociology subject (phase 4) minted openstax-intro-sociology-17-x and britannica-* ids for politics-adjacent content; political-science's OWN topics must use OpenStax American Government ids (openstax-american-government-3e-*) or mint their own — cross-subject overlap only as related-topic pointers. cautions: Ideologies: describe the spectrum factually (classical liberalism vs modern usage; conservatism, liberalism, socialism — each attributed); no endorsements; no candidates/parties in examples.
Constitution/checks-balances/federalism: teach per the primary text (constitution.congress.gov); amendments described factually; no interpretive advocacy.

Civil liberties/civil rights: factual legal history (Bill of Rights; landmark amendments 13-15, 19, 26 named factually); no current-case advocacy; the honest note that rights are contested and evolving.
Elections/voting/campaigns: descriptive mechanics (Electoral College, primaries, redistricting named factually); no partisan framing; attributed data (Pew, Census) only.
International relations/diplomacy: factual overview (sovereignty, UN system, NATO named); no foreign-policy advocacy.
Courts/judicial review: Marbury v. Madison attributed as the foundational case (1803, one line); judicial philosophy described neutrally.
